## Question 1 - data acquisition

__Describe and reflect upon a time when you obtained data from the internet using either web-scraping or an API.__

I had never used a public API before this assessment, so the experience I am describing is one I set up deliberately: I wanted to know how well OpenAQ — an open platform built to reduce inequality in access to air quality data — actually covers the world, and whether the countries it misses are the ones that need it most.

Finding the source was a process of elimination more than discovery. I drew up a shortlist (Open-Meteo, GBIF, Crossref, Wikimedia, e-Stat, ENTSO-E, OpenAQ) and tested each against three questions. Would acquisition involve real obstacles — authentication, rate limits, pagination — that I could learn from? Could the data support an argument rather than just a description? Would there be enough computation left over for the later parts of the project? Open-Meteo failed the first question: no key, no paging, nothing to reflect on. ENTSO-E probably had the richest data but issues its token in three working days. OpenAQ v3 had all the friction I was looking for, plus a licensing situation messy enough to raise genuine ethical questions. Station counts alone are meaningless without denominators, so I later added the World Bank Indicators API for population and PM2.5 exposure.

The obstacles I actually hit were mostly not the ones I had prepared for. I expected rate limits; what cost me more was the API's structure. OpenAQ v3 has no "give me this city's measurements" call — everything goes locations → sensors → measurements, and I had code half-written against the wrong assumption before a test request corrected me. The pagination metadata reports totals above a thousand as the literal string ">1000", so the number of pages cannot be computed up front; my loop simply runs until a page comes back short. Twenty-six pages later I had 25,364 stations. Requesting aggregates over raw measurements produced 408 timeouts until I switched to the server-side /days endpoints. And some problems were entirely self-made: pandas quietly read Namibia's country code "NA" as a missing value after a CSV round-trip, and getpass put its input box somewhere in VS Code where I never saw it, so I spent a while diagnosing a kernel that was not actually hung.

Two mistakes taught me more than the successes. Early on I pasted my API key into an LLM chat while debugging; nothing came of it, but I rotated the key and moved it into an environment file, and I now treat "where do secrets live" as a decision to make before writing any code, not after. Later I noticed that about a quarter of station records carry no licence field at all — so "the data is open" is a claim the platform's framing makes more confidently than its metadata supports, and my attribution goes to OpenAQ and its contributors rather than to a licence.

I used an LLM for source scouting and debugging throughout. It was genuinely fast where I could verify its output immediately, and confidently wrong where I could not — it described a v3 endpoint structure the real API does not have. The deeper risk was that it kept nudging the project towards a tidy thesis before the data had earned one. The boundary I had to draw myself: I measured one platform's coverage, not any country's monitoring capability.

## Question 2 - data wrangling, visualisation and communication

__Describe and reflect upon an occasion when you used data wrangling and visualisation to produce a data visualisation that effectively supported an argument you were making.__

The figure below comes from the same OpenAQ project as Question 1, and it carries the project's central argument: the platform built to correct inequality in air quality data reproduces that inequality in its own coverage. Concretely — the countries with the highest PM2.5 exposure are the ones with no reference-grade monitors on the platform at all, while the best-covered countries are among the cleanest.

I designed it for a specific reader: a programme officer at a funder or international agency deciding where money for monitoring infrastructure should go. That person is numerate but not technical, has perhaps thirty seconds for the figure, and needs to leave with a defensible claim rather than a methodology. Almost every design decision follows from that.

The most consequential decision was rejecting my first idea, a scatter of monitor density against PM2.5. The relationship is there, but a scatter needs a log axis to be readable — density spans four orders of magnitude — and zero cannot be plotted on a log axis. My strongest evidence is precisely the zeros: Cameroon has twenty stations, PM2.5 of 55.6 µg/m³, and not one reference monitor. A transform like log(x+1) would have kept those countries on the chart at the cost of an axis my reader would have to decode. So I inverted the problem: a two-panel bar chart where the top group is the ten highest-PM2.5 countries with zero reference monitors and the bottom group the ten best-covered, bar length encoding monitors per million people, colour encoding PM2.5. Zero is no longer an inconvenience to the axis — the absence of a bar is the message.

That choice created its own defect, which I only saw on the first render: a zero-length bar is invisible, so the colour channel — the pollution the whole argument rests on — vanished for exactly the countries that mattered. The fix was a coloured dot at the origin plus a text annotation ("0 monitors · PM2.5 55 µg/m³") for each zero row. Wrangling decisions followed the same audience logic: I restricted to countries above five million people so no bar could be dismissed as a small-state artefact, and broke ties in PM2.5 by population, so that where exposure was equal, the country with more affected people appeared.

Two honesty measures are in the figure rather than around it, because this reader will not read a methods section. The source note states that a zero means absence from OpenAQ, not absence of any national monitoring — Iran monitors its air; it simply is not on the platform — and the colour bar labels PM2.5 as a modelled, population-weighted estimate. That second caveat matters more than it looks: ground monitoring density is an input to the PM2.5 model, so my two variables are not fully independent, and a claim of correlation stronger than "coexistence" would outrun the data.

For a technical audience I would make the opposite trade: all 148 countries on a symlog scatter, the selection rule stated, uncertainty acknowledged, because that reader's first question is whether my twenty countries were cherry-picked. For a general-public version I would cut to five countries per panel and name the pollutant's health effects rather than its concentration. The bar chart is not the most information-dense view of this data — it is the version of the truth this particular reader can act on, which is what I now understand a visualisation argument to be.


![Reference-grade air quality monitoring coverage on OpenAQ versus PM2.5 exposure, countries above 5 million people. Sources: OpenAQ v3 locations API; World Bank WDI. Zero counts reflect absence from the OpenAQ platform, not necessarily absence of any national monitoring network.](figures/coverage.png){#fig-coverage width="90%"}

## Question 3 - function design and documentation

__Describe and critically reflect on the process of writing one or more pieces of code that are documented, reusable, modular and portable. In Appendix C, provide one or more code excerpts as evidence of this work.__


The function I am reflecting on is nearest_reference_km, written for the OpenAQ project behind Questions 1 and 2. It answers a question the coverage argument needed: for each of the 8,212 low-cost sensors in the inventory, how far away is the nearest of the 17,152 reference-grade monitors? The function takes two sets of coordinates in decimal degrees and returns, for every query point, the great-circle distance in kilometres to its nearest reference point. On the real inventory the answer has a long tail: the median low-cost sensor sits 6.1 km from a reference monitor, but the 90th percentile is 106 km and the furthest 2,078 km — half the network could in principle be calibrated against a neighbour, and a tail of it is entirely on its own.

The design decisions I can defend best are the ones about what the function refuses to do. It validates its inputs loudly: empty arrays, NaN coordinates, and values outside valid latitude ranges all raise ValueError with messages that say what is wrong and — for the likeliest mistake — why ("latitude outside [-90, 90] — are lat/lon swapped?"). Question 1 taught me this the hard way: pandas turned Namibia's country code into NaN without a word, and I only caught it downstream. A function another person will use should fail at the boundary, with a sentence they can act on, not propagate garbage. I also chose plain NumPy over geopy or scikit-learn's BallTree. Both would have been less code, but each is a dependency someone else has to install, and portability felt worth more than elegance for a function this small.

Two decisions concern shape rather than correctness. The pairwise distance matrix for the full inventory is about 141 million entries — over a gigabyte as floats, before intermediate arrays — so the computation is chunked, with chunk_size exposed as a parameter. The docstring states the memory formula and says explicitly that the parameter affects speed and memory but never the result; a test enforces that promise by comparing chunk_size=1 against chunk_size=1000. And the module keeps a second, deliberately naive implementation: a double loop over Python floats, orders of magnitude slower but obviously correct. It exists as the oracle the fast version is tested against on random inputs. Keeping slow code on purpose felt wrong at first; I now think deleting it would have been the mistake, because "the vectorised version agrees with the version I can read line by line" is the strongest correctness evidence I have.

Documentation follows NumPy docstring conventions — parameters, units, return shape, the exceptions raised and when — plus a worked example (London to Paris) that doubles as a doctest. Units live in the function names themselves: everything is _km, after I caught myself halfway into an interface where degrees went in and nothing said what came out.

Portability is partly the code and partly the packaging around it. The module sits in an installable package (pip install -e .), so imports work identically on any machine and there is no sys.path manipulation; dependencies are declared in pyproject.toml; and the ten tests run offline in seconds, with no API key, because a test another person cannot run is documentation of intent rather than a check.

What I would change: the antimeridian wraparound test exists because I wrote the test before trusting my own reading of the haversine formula, and that order — decide the behaviour, encode it as a test, then believe the code — is the habit I want to keep. What the function still lacks is any handling of the poles' degenerate longitudes; it is correct there, but nothing documents that I checked.

## Question 4 - profiling code performance

__Use appropriate profiling methods or tools to identify the main computational bottlenecks in the function discussed in Question 3, in terms of either execution time or memory usage. Any supporting evidence should be provided in Appendix D.__


I profiled nearest_reference_km from Question 3 — nearest reference-grade monitor for each of 8,212 low-cost sensors against 17,152 candidates, roughly 141 million distance pairs — with two instruments: wall-clock comparison against the naive double-loop implementation the module deliberately keeps, and line_profiler on both versions.

The naive version took 11.74 s for a 500-sensor subsample, an estimated 3.2 minutes for the full dataset. line_profiler located the cost precisely: 93.8% of time on the single line calling haversine_km inside the inner loop — 857,600 calls at about 1.9 µs each. The arithmetic in that call is a handful of trigonometric operations that should cost nanoseconds; nearly all of the 1.9 µs is NumPy's per-call dispatch overhead on scalar inputs. The bottleneck, in other words, was never the mathematics. It was calling a vectorised library 857,600 times with arrays of length one. Another 6.2% went on pure loop bookkeeping. This is the classic NumPy failure mode, but it was useful to see it quantified rather than assumed.

The mitigation was to make the array shapes carry the loop: broadcasting a chunk of query points against all reference points at once. The same profiler run on the chunked version shows the inverse profile — 99.1% of time inside one haversine_km call over a 2,000 × 17,152 block — which is what a healthy vectorised function looks like: time spent doing arithmetic, not organising it. The measured speedup is 63×; 0.187 s for the subsample, a few seconds for the full inventory.

Vectorising naively, though, would materialise the full 141-million-entry matrix — about 1.1 GB per intermediate array, and haversine needs several — hence the chunking. I assumed the chunk size traded memory for speed monotonically, and my docstring said so: "larger chunks are faster but use more memory." Profiling falsified my own documentation. Sweeping chunk sizes on the full dataset: 200 queries per block was fastest (2.46 s, ~27 MB); 8,212 — the whole dataset in one block — was slowest (4.97 s, ~1.1 GB), twice the runtime of the best setting. Past a few hundred rows the intermediate arrays fall out of CPU cache and the computation becomes memory-bandwidth-bound, so the extra memory buys negative speed. I have corrected the docstring to describe the measured plateau rather than my prior, and that correction is the most instructive output of the exercise: I would have shipped a confidently wrong sentence to exactly the person the documentation exists for.

Was optimisation worth it? Honestly: marginally, and only because of how the code is used. Three minutes once is acceptable; but this function runs inside a notebook that gets re-executed on every kernel restart and every upstream parameter change, and at 3.2 minutes per run it would have been the slowest step in the pipeline by an order of magnitude. At a few seconds it disappears. The trade-offs ran the other way too. I kept the readable naive version in the module as the tested oracle — a deliberate maintainability expense. And I declined the next optimisation rung, scikit-learn's BallTree with a haversine metric, which would likely beat my chunked version and replace twenty lines of mine with three of theirs — but adds a heavyweight dependency for a computation that now takes seconds, and hides the arithmetic I can currently test line-by-line against the oracle. Optimisation stopped being worth it at the point where the function ceased to be the thing I wait for; the profiler's job was to tell me where that point was.

## Question 5 - project organisation, collaboration and reproducibility.

__Describe and reflect upon how you managed your workload and file organisation to work collaboratively, openly and reproducibly during the data challenge or your research project. Any supporting evidence should be provided in Appendix E.__

The project I am reflecting on is the OpenAQ coverage analysis behind Questions 1–4: a solo project, which shaped everything about how it had to be managed. There was no one to divide tasks with, but also no one to catch my mistakes, remember my decisions, or run my code on a second machine — so the management problem became building substitutes for an absent collaborator.

Defining the project was the first real decision. I set three selection criteria before choosing a data source — enough acquisition friction to learn from, data that could carry an argument, enough computation to profile — and let them make the choice for me, including the painful part: rejecting ENTSO-E, probably the richer dataset, because its three-working-day token turnaround did not fit the deadline. Writing criteria down before looking hard at candidates was the single most useful management practice in the project. Every later scope question ("should I add a second pollutant? a time dimension?") got tested against the same three lines instead of being relitigated from scratch.

The reproducibility infrastructure was mostly standard, and I chose it for a selfish reason that turned out to be the right one: the first beneficiary of reproducible work is you, three days later. The code lives in an installable package (pip install -e .) rather than behind sys.path hacks, so imports behave identically anywhere; dependencies are pinned in pyproject.toml; the API key lives in .env, which .gitignore excludes; nbstripout keeps notebook outputs out of version control so diffs show changes to thinking rather than changes to rendering; and every API response is cached to disk. The cache was meant as politeness to a rate-limited API. It repaid itself the day my kernel died mid-analysis: the full pipeline re-ran without a network connection or a single repeated request. Similarly, the ten tests run offline with no credentials — a decision I made after realising that a test requiring my key is a test only I can run, which defeats its point. The one failure of this system was ordering: I decided where secrets live after pasting my API key into a chat window, and had to rotate it. Infrastructure decisions made reactively are made once and badly; the lesson is that "where do secrets live" belongs in the first hour of a project, next to git init.

There was one collaborator throughout: an LLM, and managing it turned out to be a genuine project-management problem rather than a tooling detail. It behaved like an extremely fast junior colleague with no accountability — excellent at generating candidate sources and debugging pagination, confidently wrong about API structure, and, more subtly, inclined to set direction. The correction was procedural, not technological: decisions moved to a written log with reasons attached (decisions.md in the repository), and anything the tool proposed had to be re-derived or verified before it counted. That log is now the backbone of this report's reflections, which is itself the lesson — in a solo project with an LLM, provenance of decisions needs managing as deliberately as provenance of data.

What I would do differently next time reduces to sequencing: secrets, caching and tests belong at the start, where they are cheap; and the audience for the final output — which I fixed embarrassingly late — belongs before the first figure, not after it.

*Supporting evidence in Appendix E.*

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

plot_df = table[(table["population"] > 5e6) & table["pm25"].notna()].copy()

# Ten highest-PM2.5 countries with zero reference-grade monitors;
# ties broken by population (more people affected first).
worst = plot_df[plot_df["reference_per_million"] == 0].nlargest(10, ["pm25", "population"])
best  = plot_df.nlargest(10, "reference_per_million")
combined = pd.concat([worst, best])

labels  = combined["country_name"].tolist()
values  = combined["reference_per_million"].to_numpy()
colours = combined["pm25"].to_numpy()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 8))
y = np.arange(len(combined))
norm = plt.Normalize(colours.min(), colours.max())
cmap = plt.cm.YlOrBr

ax.barh(y, values, color=cmap(norm(colours)), edgecolor="grey", linewidth=0.4)
ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(labels)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.axhline(len(worst) - 0.5, color="grey", linewidth=0.8)

# Zero-length bars are invisible: mark them with a PM2.5-coloured dot and
# annotate the value so the colour encoding still carries information.
xmax = values.max()
for yi, v, c in zip(y, values, colours):
    if v == 0:
        ax.scatter(0, yi, s=45, color=cmap(norm(c)), edgecolor="grey",
                   linewidth=0.4, zorder=3, clip_on=False)
        ax.annotate(f"0 monitors · PM2.5 {c:.0f} µg/m³", (0, yi),
                    xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                    va="center", fontsize=8, color="dimgrey")
    else:
        ax.annotate(f"{v:.1f}", (v, yi), xytext=(4, 0),
                    textcoords="offset points", va="center", fontsize=8)

ax.text(xmax, (len(worst) - 1) / 2, "Highest PM2.5,\nno reference monitors",
        ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, style="italic", color="dimgrey")
ax.text(xmax, len(worst) + (len(best) - 1) / 2, "Best-covered countries",
        ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9, style="italic", color="dimgrey")

ax.set_xlabel("Reference-grade monitors per million people (OpenAQ)")
ax.set_title("The most polluted air is the least monitored:\n"
             "reference-grade coverage vs PM2.5 exposure, countries > 5 M people")

sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=cmap, norm=norm)
cbar = fig.colorbar(sm, ax=ax)
cbar.set_label("Population-weighted mean annual PM2.5 exposure (µg/m³, modelled)")

fig.text(0.01, 0.01,
         "Sources: OpenAQ v3 locations API (accessed Aug 2026); World Bank WDI (population; "
         "PM2.5 mean annual exposure, EN.ATM.PM25.MC.M3).\n"
         "Zero counts reflect absence from the OpenAQ platform, not necessarily absence of "
         "any national monitoring network.",
         fontsize=7)

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("figures/coverage.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight")
```

## Appendix C {.appendix}

The distance module from src/openaq_survey/distance.py (docstrings abridged for space; full version with the naive oracle implementation in the GitHub repository), followed by an excerpt from its offline test suite.

```python
EARTH_RADIUS_KM = 6371.0088  # mean Earth radius, IUGG value


def haversine_km(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    """Great-circle distance in km. Decimal degrees in; broadcasts.

    >>> round(haversine_km(51.5074, -0.1278, 48.8575, 2.3514), 1)  # London-Paris
    343.9
    """
    lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2 = map(np.radians, (lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2))
    dlat = lat2 - lat1
    dlon = lon2 - lon1
    a = np.sin(dlat / 2) ** 2 + np.cos(lat1) * np.cos(lat2) * np.sin(dlon / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * EARTH_RADIUS_KM * np.arcsin(np.sqrt(a))


def nearest_reference_km(query_lat, query_lon, ref_lat, ref_lon, chunk_size=2000):
    """Distance from each query point to its nearest reference point, in km.

    Chunked so the ~8,000 x ~17,000 pairwise matrix never materialises:
    peak memory is chunk_size * n_ref * 8 bytes per intermediate array.
    `chunk_size` affects speed and memory only, never the result.

    Raises ValueError on empty, non-finite, or out-of-range coordinates.
    """
    query_lat = np.asarray(query_lat, dtype=float).ravel()
    query_lon = np.asarray(query_lon, dtype=float).ravel()
    ref_lat = np.asarray(ref_lat, dtype=float).ravel()
    ref_lon = np.asarray(ref_lon, dtype=float).ravel()
    _validate_coords(query_lat, query_lon, "query")
    _validate_coords(ref_lat, ref_lon, "reference")

    out = np.empty(query_lat.size, dtype=float)
    for start in range(0, query_lat.size, chunk_size):
        stop = start + chunk_size
        block = haversine_km(
            query_lat[start:stop, None], query_lon[start:stop, None],
            ref_lat[None, :], ref_lon[None, :],
        )
        out[start:stop] = block.min(axis=1)
    return out
    
def test_chunked_matches_naive_oracle():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    qlat, qlon = rng.uniform(-90, 90, 40), rng.uniform(-180, 180, 40)
    rlat, rlon = rng.uniform(-90, 90, 60), rng.uniform(-180, 180, 60)
    fast = nearest_reference_km(qlat, qlon, rlat, rlon, chunk_size=7)
    slow = nearest_reference_km_naive(qlat, qlon, rlat, rlon)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(fast, slow, rtol=1e-12)


def test_swapped_latlon_raises():
    # A longitude passed as latitude (e.g. 139.7 for Tokyo) must fail loudly.
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="swapped"):
        nearest_reference_km([139.7], [35.7], [61.0], [24.0])

```

   149    857650   47080000.0     54.9      2.7      for j in range(ref_lat.size):
